Operator:
Good day and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the StellarTech Solutions Q3 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a Q&A session. Today's call is being recorded.
I would now like to hand the call over to Jessica Morales, Investor Relations Director. Please go ahead.

Jessica Morales, Investor Relations Director:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and welcome to StellarTech Solutions’ third quarter earnings call. Joining me today are Alex Ramsey, CEO; Ben Carter, CFO; and Sarah Chen, Chief Technology Officer.
Earlier today, we published our earnings press release and presentation, which are available on our Investor Relations site. Today’s discussion may include forward-looking statements. With that, let me turn the call over to Alex.

Alex Ramsey, Chief Executive Officer:
Thanks, Jessica, and welcome everyone.

We’re pleased with our performance this quarter, despite some headwinds in certain segments. I want to highlight a few areas:

This quarter, we've seen some significant movement regarding government grants, local grants, tax incentives, and loans. Let me give a detailed explanation of the impact of these factors on StellarTech Korea's Q4 financial performance, particularly focusing on the effects of the dividend exclusion reform. As initially indicated, Q4 2024 saw a net income of KRW 23.8 trillion. This figure, while positive, requires nuanced understanding. A significant driver of this net income increase was the newly implemented dividend exclusion measure. This measure, designed to incentivize repatriation of profits from overseas subsidiaries, allows for the exclusion of a portion of dividends received from corporate tax calculations. Specifically, the reform allows for a 95% exclusion of dividends received from subsidiaries located in jurisdictions with a tax treaty with Korea, and an 80% exclusion from subsidiaries in jurisdictions without a tax treaty, provided the subsidiary meets certain minimum ownership thresholds, typically 20% ownership for at least one year prior to dividend payment. Before this reform, Korean companies were essentially disincentivized from repatriating profits due to the high tax burden. Now, with this exclusion, we saw a marked increase in dividend repatriation in Q4. We estimate that approximately KRW 15 trillion in dividends were repatriated in Q4, compared to an average of KRW 8 trillion per quarter in the previous year. This KRW 7 trillion increase in dividend repatriation directly contributed to the higher net income figure. The Korean government also offers a variety of tax incentives beyond the dividend exclusion, broadly aimed at promoting investment in key sectors such as semiconductors, biotechnology, and renewable energy. The Investment Tax Credit (ITC) for semiconductor manufacturing, which offers a tax credit of up to 15% for investments in new semiconductor manufacturing facilities, continued to spur significant investment in this critical sector. We observed that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix collectively invested over KRW 12 trillion in new fabrication plants in Q4, leveraging this incentive. We project this incentive will increase Korea's market share in advanced chip manufacturing by 2% by the end of 2025. The R&D tax credit, which provides a tax credit for qualified R&D expenditures, has been instrumental in fostering innovation. We noted a 20% increase in R&D spending across the tech sector in Q4, with companies like LG Chem and Hyundai Motor Group significantly increasing their R&D budgets, directly attributable to the improved tax environment. Several smaller companies were able to benefit from the Tax Credit Refund Program, which allowed companies to apply for a refund on previously accrued tax credits. The intention behind this program was to infuse smaller businesses with capital, and according to our analysis, the average tax refund for this quarter was KRW 5.2 billion per business. In addition to national-level incentives, local governments also offer a range of tax incentives to attract investment. For example, the Gyeonggi Province offers significant tax breaks for companies establishing operations in its special economic zones, particularly those focused on advanced materials and components. We saw a 15% increase in Q3 revenue year-over-year to $2.3 billion, stemming from the ITC investments in these regions. Beyond tax incentives, direct government grants played a crucial role in specific sectors. The government allocated KRW 3 trillion in grants to support the transition to renewable energy sources. These grants were specifically targeted at companies developing solar, wind, and hydrogen technologies. For example, the Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) received a significant grant to develop a large-scale offshore wind farm off the coast of Jeju Island. Local governments across Korea provide grants to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to support innovation and growth. These grants typically range from KRW 50 million to KRW 500 million and are designed to help SMEs commercialize new technologies and expand their operations. We've seen a positive correlation between these grants and job creation in smaller cities, with an estimated 15,000 jobs created as a direct result of these grants in Q4. The Ministry of Science and ICT introduced a Digital New Deal initiative involving a mixture of grants and low-interest loans to promote the adoption of digital technologies across various industries. This has led to a surge in investment in areas such as artificial intelligence, big data, and cloud computing. The Korean government also utilizes strategic loan programs to support specific industries and projects. The Korea Export-Import Bank (KEXIM) provides financing to Korean companies undertaking overseas projects. This financing helps Korean companies compete more effectively in the global market and supports the export of Korean goods and services. In Q4, KEXIM provided over KRW 5 trillion in financing to support Korean companies building infrastructure projects in Southeast Asia. The Small and Medium Business Corporation (SBC) provides policy loans to SMEs at below-market interest rates. These loans are designed to help SMEs access capital and grow their businesses. We've seen a positive impact from these loans, with a notable increase in SMEs expanding their operations and hiring new employees. Focusing specifically on the tax refund for this quarter, we saw a higher-than-anticipated volume of tax refunds processed. This was due to a combination of factors, including increased tax credit utilization, the dividend repatriation impact, and government stimulus measures. In response to concerns about slowing economic growth, the government implemented temporary measures to accelerate tax refunds. The combined effect of these government initiatives and tax reforms has been a positive one, contributing to increased investment, innovation, and job creation. However, it's important to note some potential challenges, including the sustainability of incentives, competition with other economies, and the global economic slowdown. We recommend continued monitoring of the effectiveness of these government initiatives and tax reforms. It is crucial to analyze the long-term impact on the Korean economy and to make adjustments as needed. Further, businesses should actively engage with government agencies to understand and leverage these incentives to their full potential.

Let's turn to our CapEx and the comments on it for this quarter. StellarTech Electronics' Capital Expenditure (CapEx) for the fourth quarter of 2023 totaled KRW 20.2 trillion, representing a strategic investment in future growth and technological leadership. This robust CapEx reflects KoreTech's commitment to maintaining its competitive edge in the memory, foundry, and display sectors. A substantial KRW 18.8 trillion was allocated to the DS (Device Solutions) division, with KRW 0.4 trillion directed towards Display. The focus within DS was primarily on advancing memory technology, expanding foundry capacity, and laying the groundwork for future manufacturing capabilities. The lion's share of memory CapEx, approximately 62% or KRW 7.75 trillion, was dedicated to preparations for advanced memory technologies, specifically focusing on next-generation DRAM and NAND flash memory. This includes investment in the P3 and P4 infrastructure. These fabs are crucial for scaling production of DDR5 DRAM and 232-layer (and beyond) NAND flash memory. A critical component of this advanced technology push was investment in Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography equipment. We deployed an additional 3 EUV scanners at P3 and 2 at P4, bringing our total EUV scanner count to 18 across our memory production facilities. This expansion is expected to allow us to increase EUV-based production by 25% in H1 2024. We expect this improved efficiency to reduce per-bit manufacturing cost by approximately 8% in 2024. KRW 0.5 trillion was allocated to pilot lines focused on exploring next-generation memory technologies beyond the immediate roadmap, including research into MRAM (Magnetoresistive RAM) and ReRAM (Resistive RAM) as potential future memory solutions. The majority of foundry CapEx, roughly 70% or KRW 4.41 trillion, focused on expanding production capacity for advanced nodes (5nm and below) at the Pyeongtaek site. Specifically, the new line at Pyeongtaek is expected to come online in Q2 2024, adding approximately 30,000 wafers per month (WPM) of capacity. A significant portion of the investment, KRW 1.26 trillion, was dedicated to establishing initial capacity for 3-nanometer process technology. While 3nm yields are still in the early stages, we are seeing strong interest from customers in high-performance computing (HPC) and mobile applications. We anticipate ramping 3nm production throughout 2024, targeting full capacity utilization by late 2024/early 2025. CapEx also included initial infrastructure development for the new Taylor, Texas fabrication plant. This involved land preparation, utility connections, and initial building construction. The Taylor site represents a critical strategic investment in securing access to the US market and diversifying our manufacturing footprint. Approximately KRW 0.63 trillion was spent in this area. A substantial portion of display CapEx, KRW 0.25 trillion, was invested in expanding the production capacity for flexible OLED displays. This expansion is targeted at meeting growing demand from the smartphone and automotive sectors. Specifically, we added a new module line dedicated to under-panel camera technology for foldable displays. The remaining CapEx, KRW 0.15 trillion, was allocated to facility improvements in infrastructure, including upgrades to cleanrooms and power systems to enhance production efficiency and yield.

I’ll now pass it over to Ben to walk through the numbers in more detail.

Ben Carter, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Alex, and hello, everyone.

Let me break it down starting with the gross margin results. In Q3 2023, our consolidated gross profit reached KRW 21.8 trillion, a decrease of KRW 6.9 trillion compared to the KRW 28.7 trillion reported in Q2 2023. This translates to a gross margin of 31%, a significant decline of 6.4 percentage points from the 37.4% achieved in the previous quarter. This performance fell short of our Q2 guidance of 34-35%. The primary drivers behind the QoQ decline in gross profit and margin can be attributed to the Memory division price decline and inventory valuation loss, which had a 60% impact. The Memory division experienced a sharper-than-anticipated price decline across all major DRAM and NAND product categories. The average selling price (ASP) for DRAM decreased by approximately 18% QoQ, driven by weaker demand in the PC and mobile segments, coupled with increased industry supply. NAND flash ASPs saw an even steeper decline of 22% QoQ, reflecting persistent oversupply and aggressive pricing strategies from competitors. This price erosion, compounded by an inventory valuation loss of KRW 2.8 trillion, significantly impacted the Memory division's profitability. This inventory write-down reflects the lowered market value of existing inventory due to the continued price decreases. We initiated a strategic shift towards higher-density, higher-value products in Q3, but the immediate impact on ASPs was limited. For example, our transition to 1alpha nm DRAM production, while technically successful, yielded lower initial yields than projected, adding to the cost burden. Smartphone sales weakness had a 30% impact, with our Mobile eXperience (MX) division facing challenges in Q3 due to softer-than-expected demand for our flagship and mid-range smartphone models, particularly in developed markets like North America and Europe. While the launch of our new foldable devices (Galaxy Z Fold 5 and Flip 5) generated positive initial traction, overall smartphone shipments decreased by approximately 8% QoQ. This volume decline, coupled with increased promotional activities to maintain market share amidst intensifying competition from Chinese manufacturers, further compressed gross margins. Specifically, increased component costs for the camera modules in the premium models impacted margins. Increased component costs, with a 10% impact, saw rising costs of key components, including displays and advanced application processors (APs), put further strain on the gross margin, especially in the MX division. While we secured some cost savings through supply chain diversification efforts, the overall impact was insufficient to offset the price increases in certain critical components. We are actively negotiating long-term supply agreements to mitigate future cost pressures. Compared to Q3 2022, gross profit decreased by KRW 11.2 trillion (from KRW 33.0 trillion), and gross margin declined by 9.5 percentage points (from 40.5%). This YoY decline reflects a broader industry downturn. The global memory market experienced a significant slowdown compared to the robust demand seen in Q3 2022. The global economic uncertainty, impacting consumer spending and enterprise IT investments, led to a sharp decrease in demand for memory products. Weakened consumer confidence in Europe and North America due to inflation and rising interest rates created less spending in the technology sectors. Increased tensions between the US and China, as well as the war in Ukraine had a negative impact on supply chain efficiencies. Our Q3 2023 gross margin of 31% fell short of our Q2 guidance of 34-35%. We had anticipated a price decline in the Memory division, but the actual decline exceeded our expectations due to a faster-than-anticipated increase in industry supply and weaker-than-expected demand. Our initial models projected a 12% decline in DRAM ASPs, but the actual decline was 18%. We now acknowledge that our demand forecast was overly optimistic, particularly regarding PC and mobile DRAM demand. We had projected a stronger performance in the MX division, driven by the launch of our new foldable devices. However, the actual sales volume was lower than expected due to increased competition and weaker consumer sentiment in key markets. The Galaxy Z Fold 5 and Flip 5, while well-received, did not fully offset the decline in sales of other smartphone models. We had anticipated a shipment volume of 78 million units, but the actual shipment volume was closer to 72 million units. We initiated several cost-cutting measures in Q2, including optimization of manufacturing processes and reduction in operating expenses. However, the full impact of these measures will not be realized until Q4 2023 and beyond. For example, the transition of our NAND flash production to a more cost-efficient node experienced delays due to technical challenges.

Now, moving to the operating margin results, which we’ve been tracking closely. The Company's Q2 2024 operating margin was 6.1%, a decrease of 8 percentage points compared to Q1 2024 (14.1%). This decline reflects a significant drop in operating profit, which fell KRW 6.5 trillion sequentially from KRW 10.8 trillion in Q1 2024 to KRW 4.3 trillion in Q2 2024. This performance fell short of the guidance provided in the Q1 2024 earnings call, which projected an operating margin of 8.5% - 9.5%. The primary drivers for this underperformance were a substantial reduction in Memory division profitability and a contraction in the Mobile eXperience (MX) division's profitability due to diminishing new product launch momentum. The operating margin was 6.1% in Q2 2024 versus 14.1% in Q1 2024, a decrease of 8 percentage points. The operating profit was KRW 4.3 trillion in Q2 2024 versus KRW 10.8 trillion in Q1 2024, a decrease of KRW 6.5 trillion. While consolidated revenue showed a slight increase of 2% QoQ (from KRW 76 trillion in Q1 2024 to KRW 77.5 trillion in Q2 2024), the disproportionate decline in operating profit led to the significant margin contraction. The Memory division experienced a sharp decline in profitability. Average Selling Prices (ASPs) for DRAM declined by approximately 18% QoQ due to oversupply in the market and a slowdown in demand from PC and smartphone manufacturers. NAND Flash ASPs also decreased by 12% QoQ, further impacting the division's operating profit. Specifically, Memory division operating profit plunged from KRW 7 trillion in Q1 to KRW 2.5 trillion in Q2. This was despite a 5% QoQ increase in overall memory bit shipments, indicating that price erosion significantly outweighed volume gains. The MX division experienced a decline in operating profit from KRW 3 trillion in Q1 to KRW 2 trillion in Q2. This was primarily due to the waning impact of the flagship smartphone launches in Q1. While the initial sales figures were strong, demand softened in Q2, particularly in the premium segment. Marketing expenses also increased by 10% QoQ to support the launch of mid-range devices and maintain market share, further impacting the division's profitability. The operating margin was 6.1% in Q2 2024 versus 10.5% in Q2 2023, a decrease of 4.4 percentage points. The operating profit was KRW 4.3 trillion in Q2 2024 versus KRW 7.5 trillion in Q2 2023, a decrease of KRW 3.2 trillion. Revenue decreased by 5% YoY (from KRW 81.5 trillion in Q2 2023 to KRW 77.5 trillion in Q2 2024). The YoY decline reflects the challenging macroeconomic environment, characterized by high inflation, rising interest rates, and geopolitical uncertainties, which have dampened consumer spending and enterprise IT investment. Intensified competition in both the Memory and MX markets has also contributed to the margin pressure. In the Memory sector, aggressive pricing strategies by competitors aiming to gain market share further eroded ASPs. In the MX division, the increased presence of Chinese smartphone manufacturers with competitive offerings has impacted sales volumes and required increased marketing investments. Performance varied across regions. While North America and Europe showed relative resilience, demand in China and emerging markets experienced a sharper decline due to economic slowdowns and currency fluctuations. Specifically, revenue in China decreased by 12% YoY. The actual operating margin fell significantly short of the guidance due to several factors. The initial guidance assumed a more stable memory market with a gradual recovery in demand in the second half of the year. However, the oversupply situation worsened in Q2, leading to steeper-than-anticipated price declines. The guidance assumed DRAM ASPs would only decline by 8% QoQ; the actual decline was 18%. The sales mix in the MX division shifted towards mid-range devices, which have lower profit margins compared to flagship models. This was partly due to weaker-than-expected demand for premium smartphones in key markets. The guidance assumed a more balanced sales mix. Unexpectedly high inflationary pressures led to increased component costs and logistics expenses, further impacting the operating margin. The guidance factored in a certain level of inflation, but the actual impact was more pronounced.

Lastly, I'd like to briefly touch on sales by segment or platforms. Q3 2024 presented a mixed bag of results across Samsung's diverse portfolio. While certain segments, particularly Foundry, VD, and Harman, delivered strong performance, others, including Memory, System LSI, MX, and Digital Appliances, faced significant headwinds. Overall, the corporation demonstrated resilience amidst global economic uncertainties, but strategic adjustments are necessary to navigate evolving market dynamics. Memory division revenue plummeted by 28% year-over-year to $18.5 billion. Operating profit swung to a loss of $1.2 billion, a stark contrast to the $5.8 billion profit in Q3 2023. Gross margin declined significantly from 45% to 22%, primarily due to a steep Average Selling Price (ASP) decrease of 22% across DRAM and NAND Flash products. A further 5% margin hit was attributed to a $750 million inventory valuation loss, reflecting the impact of rapid price declines and oversupply in the market. Earnings in System LSI were adversely affected by customers' inventory adjustments in the mobile application processor (AP) and image sensor segments. While our 200MP image sensor continues to gain traction, overall sales were subdued. Revenue decreased by 15% year-over-year to $6.8 billion. Operating profit declined by 30% to $840 million. Foundry achieved exceptional results, driven by strong demand for our advanced process technologies, particularly in the 5nm and 4nm nodes. We are seeing increased adoption from customers in the HPC (High-Performance Computing), AI, and automotive segments. Record-high quarterly revenue of $7.5 billion, up 18% year-over-year. Operating profit increased by 25% to $1.5 billion. Overall, the display division revenue was flat year-over-year at $8.2 billion. Operating profit decreased by 10% to $900 million. The mobile panel business faced challenges due to reduced demand from smartphone manufacturers, impacting profitability. However, our large panel business narrowed its losses, driven by improved yield rates and increased demand for premium OLED TVs. The MX business experienced a slowdown in Q3 due to the waning launch effects of new flagship devices and weak demand in the mid-to-low-end segment, particularly in emerging markets. Revenue declined by 8% year-over-year to $26 billion. Operating profit decreased by 15% to $3.5 billion. The Network division delivered solid growth, driven by strong domestic demand for 5G infrastructure deployments and business expansion overseas, particularly in Europe and Southeast Asia. Revenue increased by 12% year-over-year to $2.5 billion. Operating profit increased by 10% to $250 million. The VD division achieved strong results, driven by proactive efforts to address year-end seasonal demand and increased sales of premium products, including Neo QLED and Micro LED TVs. Revenue increased by 10% year-over-year to $12 billion. Operating profit increased by 15% to $1.8 billion. The Digital Appliances division faced significant headwinds due to deteriorating market conditions, including rising inflation and weak consumer confidence. Revenue decreased by 5% year-over-year to $6.5 billion. Operating profit decreased by 20% to $650 million. Harman delivered exceptional results, driven by increased revenue in the automotive business and solid sales of consumer audio products. Record-high quarterly profit for the second consecutive quarter, with revenue up 15% year-over-year to $3.8 billion. Operating profit up 20% to $450 million.

Now, let me hand things over to Sarah to talk about product and operational progress.

Sarah Chen, Chief Technology Officer:
Thanks, Ben.

This was a busy quarter for our teams. On the innovation front, we made meaningful advances around our next-generation AI inference engine. This included the release of StellarInfer, which is already demonstrating significant performance gains in our cloud infrastructure.

Also worth noting is our aggressive CapEx in advanced technologies. Our memory division continues to see strong long-term demand. While Q4 saw a slight dip in average selling price (ASP) for DRAM (approximately -3% QoQ), NAND ASP remained relatively stable. This is due to the impact of increased supply-chain competition, in particular in the NAND flash sector. Our aggressive CapEx in advanced technologies is designed to ensure we remain cost-competitive and technologically ahead of our rivals. We anticipate that the market will begin to tighten in H2 2024, driving better ASPs and improving profitability. The foundry business experienced a 15% increase in Q3 revenue year-over-year to KRW 2.3 trillion. This growth is primarily driven by strong demand for our 5nm process. We are actively working to secure additional design wins for our 3nm node, and we are confident in our ability to compete effectively in the advanced node market. The investment in the Taylor site is critical to mitigating geopolitical risks and securing access to key customers in North America. This initiative is expected to qualify for significant government incentives, which will help offset the initial investment costs. The display division saw a 7% decrease in revenue year-over-year in Q4, largely due to increased competition from Chinese display manufacturers. However, we are focusing on differentiating ourselves through superior technology and higher-value applications, such as foldable displays and automotive displays. The CapEx investments are designed to enhance our technological leadership and maintain our position as a premium display provider.

And we’ve made foundational changes in how we approach our foundry customer relationships, particularly on the fulfillment and logistics side. Our analysis suggests that the "foundry customer" is a major automotive Tier 1 supplier, most likely focused on ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems) and potentially even early-stage autonomous driving applications. The design win itself likely encompasses a System-on-Chip (SoC) for next-generation automotive platforms, handling sensor fusion, perception algorithms, and potentially even vehicle control functions. The customer's transition from 5nm mass production to 4nm development is a significant indicator of several key trends. ADAS and autonomous driving systems are incredibly compute-intensive. The move to 4nm allows for a significantly higher transistor density, resulting in improved performance and reduced power consumption compared to the 5nm node. We estimate a performance boost of roughly 15-20% with a corresponding 10-12% reduction in power consumption based on industry benchmarks. This is critical for automotive applications where heat dissipation and energy efficiency are paramount. The 4nm process allows for the integration of more complex functionalities on a single chip. This includes advanced AI accelerators, dedicated image signal processors (ISPs) for camera input, and high-bandwidth interfaces for connecting to sensors like LiDAR and radar. This integrated approach not only reduces the bill of materials (BOM) but also improves system latency and overall performance. Automotive lifecycles are notoriously long. Automakers need to ensure that the components they use today will be supported and available for years to come. By investing in 4nm now, our foundry customer is securing their technology roadmap and demonstrating a commitment to long-term product support. They are likely planning for model year 2026-2028 vehicles with these 4nm based systems. We project this design win to contribute significantly to the foundry's revenue stream over the next 3-5 years. Based on our models, we anticipate the 5nm mass production for this automotive customer to have generated approximately $180 - $220 million in revenue for the foundry in the current fiscal year (FY2024). This is a conservative estimate assuming initial ramp-up volumes. The 4nm development phase will involve smaller initial orders for prototyping and testing, but we foresee a rapid ramp-up in production volumes by FY2026, potentially leading to a 25-30% increase in revenue from this customer compared to the 5nm node at peak production. This translates to a potential revenue stream of $225 - $286 million annually from this single design win at full production capacity. The 4nm process, being at the cutting edge, will likely command a higher gross margin compared to the more mature 5nm process. We estimate a 3-5 percentage point increase in gross margin for the foundry on these 4nm automotive chips. This is driven by the higher ASP (Average Selling Price) and the value-added features enabled by the advanced node. We understand that this specific automotive customer has a strong presence in the European and North American markets. Therefore, the demand for these 4nm chips will likely be concentrated in these regions initially. However, as autonomous driving technology becomes more widespread, we expect to see increased demand from Asian markets as well, specifically China and Japan. The foundry's ability to effectively manage its global supply chain and cater to the specific needs of each region will be crucial for maximizing the potential of this design win. We will emphasize our technological prowess in advanced node manufacturing and our ability to meet the stringent requirements of the automotive industry (e.g., high reliability, long product lifecycles, and compliance with automotive safety standards like ISO 26262). We are likely to mention specific process enhancements tailored to automotive applications, such as improved memory reliability and enhanced security features. The commentary will underscore the strong partnership between the foundry and the automotive customer, emphasizing the collaborative efforts in design optimization, process customization, and quality assurance. This will reinforce our commitment to providing a holistic solution beyond just manufacturing. We will frame this design win as a key milestone in our strategy to capture a larger share of the rapidly growing automotive semiconductor market. We might mention ongoing investments in R&D to develop even more advanced process technologies for future automotive applications, such as 3nm and beyond. We could also highlight initiatives focused on automotive-specific IP (Intellectual Property) development, such as specialized AI accelerators and sensor interface solutions. Expect the commentary to address the ongoing concerns surrounding supply chain resilience. We will likely mention our efforts to diversify our manufacturing footprint and secure access to critical raw materials to ensure a stable supply of chips for our automotive customers, even in the face of geopolitical uncertainties. This could involve expanding capacity in different geographical locations or forging strategic partnerships with key suppliers.

Let’s now open the floor for questions.

Q&A SESSION

Analyst 1:
Hi, thanks for taking my question. On the foundry customer design win, could you expand on what’s driving that strength?

Alex Ramsey:
Certainly. We are seeing increased adoption from customers in the HPC (High-Performance Computing), AI, and automotive segments. Our focus on expanding our capacity and enhancing our technology leadership is paying off. We are accelerating the development and deployment of 3nm and 2nm process technologies to maintain a competitive edge. We are expanding foundry capacity in the United States to address growing demand and geopolitical considerations. We are strengthening partnerships with leading EDA (Electronic Design Automation) vendors to streamline the design process for customers.

Analyst 2:
A follow-up on operating margin. How confident are you that your production adjustments will have the desired effect?

Ben Carter:
We are implementing production cuts to reduce inventory levels and stabilize ASPs. The Company plans to reduce DRAM and NAND flash production by approximately 10% and 15%, respectively, in the second half of the year. We are shifting focus towards high-value, high-performance memory solutions, such as HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) for AI applications and enterprise SSDs. This segment currently represents 15% of Memory revenue but boasts margins 5-7 percentage points higher than standard DRAM. We are accelerating the development and deployment of next-generation memory technologies, such as DDR6 and V7 NAND, to maintain a competitive edge.

Analyst 3:
And for the AI inference engine, any update on the timeline for broader deployment?

Sarah Chen:
We are currently integrating StellarInfer across our entire cloud infrastructure. We anticipate a full rollout by the end of Q1 next year, which will allow us to significantly reduce our operational costs and improve the performance of our AI services.

Analyst 4:
Just a final one — on the gross margin, is the improvement mostly driven by cost-cutting measures or are you expecting some ASP recovery as well?

Ben Carter:
We are actively adjusting our memory production capacity to better align with market demand and reduce inventory levels. We announced a further 5% reduction in DRAM wafer starts in Q3 and plan to implement additional reductions in Q4. We are enhancing product differentiation in the MX division, particularly in the premium segment, by introducing innovative features and designs. We are also exploring new form factors and technologies to capture emerging market opportunities. We are intensifying our efforts to optimize costs across all business units, including streamlining operations, improving manufacturing efficiency, and negotiating favorable supply agreements. While cost-cutting is a major component, we are expecting some ASP recovery as well, particularly in the memory division, as supply and demand become more balanced.

Closing

Alex Ramsey:
Thank you again for joining us today. We remain confident in our long-term growth story and are committed to disciplined execution. We appreciate your continued interest and support.

Operator:
Thank you. This concludes today’s call. You may now disconnect.

aspect_summary.CapEx, and the CapEx comments for this q: StellarTech Electronics' CapEx for Q4 2023 totaled KRW 20.2 trillion, with KRW 18.8 trillion allocated to the DS division and KRW 0.4 trillion to Display. Memory CapEx focused on advanced technologies, including DDR5 DRAM and 232-layer NAND flash memory, with investments in P3 and P4 infrastructure and EUV lithography equipment (5 new EUV scanners added). Foundry CapEx focused on expanding production capacity for advanced nodes (5nm and below) at the Pyeongtaek site, including 3nm process technology. CapEx also included initial infrastructure development for the Taylor, Texas fabrication plant. Display CapEx expanded flexible OLED display production capacity and facility improvements.
aspect_summary.Operating margin results, QoQ changes, Y: The company's Q2 2024 operating margin was 6.1%, a decrease of 8 percentage points compared to Q1 2024 (14.1%). Operating profit fell KRW 6.5 trillion sequentially, from KRW 10.8 trillion to KRW 4.3 trillion. This performance fell short of the Q1 2024 guidance of 8.5% - 9.5%. The primary drivers for this underperformance were a substantial reduction in Memory division profitability and a contraction in the Mobile eXperience (MX) division's profitability. Compared to Q2 2023, the operating margin decreased by 4.4 percentage points (from 10.5% to 6.1%), and operating profit decreased by KRW 3.2 trillion (from KRW 7.5 trillion to KRW 4.3 trillion). Revenue decreased by 5% YoY. The actual operating margin fell significantly short of the guidance due to a more unstable memory market, a shift in the sales mix in the MX division, and unexpectedly high inflationary pressures.
aspect_summary.Gross margin results, QoQ changes, YoY c: In Q3 2023, the consolidated gross margin was 31%, a decrease of 6.4 percentage points from the 37.4% in Q2 2023. Gross profit reached KRW 21.8 trillion, a decrease of KRW 6.9 trillion compared to Q2. This fell short of the Q2 guidance of 34-35%. The QoQ decline was primarily due to price declines and inventory valuation losses in the Memory division (60% impact), weaker smartphone sales (30% impact), and increased component costs (10% impact). Compared to Q3 2022, the gross margin declined by 9.5 percentage points (from 40.5%), and gross profit decreased by KRW 11.2 trillion. The Q3 2023 gross margin of 31% fell short of the Q2 guidance of 34-35% because the price decline in the Memory division exceeded expectations, and smartphone sales were lower than expected.
